My current finding is that the condition “there exist β, k≠ℓ with Sₙ(α)⋆β=1 iff n∈{k,ℓ} and 0 otherwise’’ is equivalent to the existence of an integer vector β such that the cross‑correlation of α (supported on {0,…,8}) with β equals the sum of two unit impulses:  

\[
c(n)=\sum_{t\in\mathbb Z}\alpha(t+n)\beta(t)=\delta_{n,k}+\delta_{n,\ell}.
\]

Thus the problem reduces to: **find all integer 9‑vectors α=(α₀,…,α₈) for which the linear map β↦c (correlation) can produce a sequence with exactly two entries equal to 1 and all others 0.** This reformulation turns the original combinatorial description into a linear‑algebraic feasibility problem.

My current finding is that the condition “\(S_n(\alpha)\star\beta=1\) for exactly two shifts \(k\neq l\) and \(0\) otherwise” is equivalent to the existence of an integer sequence \(b\) (the reversed \(\beta\)) such that the convolution  

\[
(a*b)(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}a_i\,b_{\,n-i}
\]

equals the indicator function \(\mathbf 1_{\{k,l\}}\).  Thus a shifty \(\alpha\) is precisely a length‑9 integer vector \(a=(a_0,\dots,a_8)\) for which there exists a finitely‑supported integer vector \(b\) solving the linear system  

\[
\begin{cases}
\sum_{i=0}^{8}a_i\,b_{k-i}=1,\\[2mm]
\sum_{i=0}^{8}a_i\,b_{l-i}=1,\\[2mm]
\sum_{i=0}^{8}a_i\,b_{n-i}=0\quad\text{for all other }n.
\end{cases}
\]

In other words, \(\alpha\) must be a divisor (over \(\mathbb Z\)) of a two‑point “spike’’ sequence. This reduction to a convolution/divisibility problem is the key step for counting all such \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that the condition “there exist β and distinct k,l with Sₙ(α)⋆β =1 iff n∈{k,l}” is equivalent to the existence of an integer‑valued sequence β̃ (the reversal of β) such that the discrete convolution  

\[
(\alpha * \betã)(n)=\sum_{t=0}^{8}\alpha(t)\,\betã(n-t)=\delta_{k}(n)+\delta_{l}(n)
\]

holds for all n. In other words, a shifty α is precisely a length‑9 integer vector whose convolution with some other integer vector yields a two‑point delta (value 1 at two distinct indices and 0 elsewhere). This reformulation reduces the problem to finding all α∈ℤ⁹ for which the linear Diophantine system  

\[
\sum_{t=0}^{8}\alpha(t)\,\betã(n-t)=\begin{cases}1&n=k,l\\0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}
\]

has an integer solution β̃ and distinct integers k,l. This is the key reduction that will allow us to count the admissible α.

My current finding is that the condition for a “shifty’’ function \(\alpha\) can be written as a convolution equation  

\[
\sum_{i=0}^{8}a_i\,\beta(i-n)=\delta_{n,k}+\delta_{n,l}\qquad(\forall n\in\mathbb Z),
\]

where \(a_i=\alpha(i)\) and \(\beta\) is an arbitrary finitely‑supported integer sequence.  In generating‑function form this is  

\[
A(x)\,B(x^{-1})=x^{-k}+x^{-l},
\]

with \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}a_i x^i\) and \(B(x)=\sum_{t}\beta(t)x^t\).  Thus \(\alpha\) is shifty iff its polynomial \(A(x)\) divides a two‑term Laurent polynomial \(x^{-k}+x^{-l}\) in \(\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\).  This reduction to a divisibility problem is the key step toward counting all possible \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that a shifty \(\alpha\) corresponds exactly to a Laurent‑polynomial divisor of a two‑point spike: writing \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}a_i x^i\) and \(B(x)=\sum_j b_j x^j\), the condition is  
\[
A(x)B(x)=x^k+x^l\qquad(k\neq l),
\]  
so \(A(x)=x^rC(x)\) where \(C(x)\mid(1+x^q)\) in \(\mathbb Z[x]\) with \(q=|k-l|>0\) and the shift \(r\) is chosen so that all exponents of \(A\) lie in \(\{0,\dots,8\}\). Thus counting shifty functions reduces to counting all integer‑coefficient divisors \(C(x)\) of \(1+x^q\) (including \(\pm1\)) whose monomial shift fits into the interval \([0,8]\). This reduction to a divisor‑of‑\(1+x^q\) problem is the key step.

My current finding is that a shifty α exists **iff** its generating polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\in\mathbb Z[x]
\]

is a (primitive) divisor of a binomial \(x^{d}+1\) for some non‑zero integer \(d\).  
Indeed, writing \(\beta'(j)=\beta(-j)\) gives the convolution equation  

\[
\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)\beta'(n-i)=\delta_{n,k}+\delta_{n,\ell}
\]

which in generating‑function form is  

\[
A(x)\,B'(x)=x^{k}+x^{\ell}=x^{k}\bigl(1+x^{d}\bigr),\qquad d=\ell-k\neq0.
\]

Since \(x^{k}\) is a unit in \(\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\), the condition reduces to  

\[
A(x)\mid\bigl(1+x^{d}\bigr)\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}].
\]

Thus counting shifty functions is equivalent to counting all primitive integer polynomials of degree ≤ 8 that divide some \(x^{d}+1\) (up to a sign). This reduction to a divisibility problem is the key step.

My current finding is that the shifty condition is equivalent to the existence of integers \(d>0\) and a polynomial \(B(x)\in\mathbb Z[x]\) with non‑zero constant term such that  

\[
A(x)=x^{r}B(x),\qquad B(x)\mid (1+x^{d})\ \text{in }\mathbb Z[x],
\]

where \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\) and \(r=\min\{i:\alpha(i)\neq0\}\).  In other words, every shifty \(\alpha\) is obtained by taking a divisor \(B\) of a binomial \(1+x^{d}\) (with \(d\le 8\) because \(\deg A\le8\)) and optionally multiplying by a monomial \(x^{r}\) (shifting the support).  This reduction replaces the original functional condition by a simple divisibility problem.

My current finding is that the shifty condition is equivalent to a divisibility condition on the polynomial \(A(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)z^{i}\): there must exist a positive integer \(m\) such that  

\[
A(z)\mid(z^{m}+1)\qquad\text{in }\mathbb Z[z].
\]

Indeed, writing \(\beta\) as a Laurent polynomial \(B(z)=\sum_{j} \beta(j)z^{j}\), the correlation identity \(S_{n}(\alpha)\star\beta=\delta_{n,k}+\delta_{n,\ell}\) becomes \(A(z)B(z)=z^{k}+z^{\ell}=z^{\ell}(z^{|k-\ell|}+1)\); since monomials are units in \(\mathbb Z[z,z^{-1}]\), this is equivalent to \(A(z)\mid(z^{m}+1)\) with \(m=|k-\ell|>0\). Thus counting shifty \(\alpha\) reduces to counting integer polynomials of degree ≤ 8 that divide some binomial \(z^{m}+1\).

My current finding is that a shifty α exists **iff** its generating polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\in\mathbb Z[x]
\]

is a (primitive) divisor of a binomial \(x^{d}+1\) for some non‑zero integer \(d\).  Equivalently, \(A(x)\) must be a product of distinct cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{r}(x)\) with even index \(r\) (since every even‑indexed cyclotomic appears in some \(x^{d}+1\)), and the total degree \(\sum_{r\in S}\varphi(r)\) of the chosen factors must be \(\le8\).  Thus counting shifty functions reduces to counting all subsets \(S\) of even integers whose totient‑degrees sum to at most 8 (including the empty set), and then multiplying by 2 for the overall sign of \(A\).

My current finding is that the “shifty’’ condition is **exactly** the divisibility condition  

\[
A(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)z^{i}\;\mid\;z^{m}+1\qquad(m\ge1)
\]

in the integer polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[z]\).  Indeed, writing \(\beta\) as a Laurent polynomial \(B(z)=\sum_{j}\beta(j)z^{j}\) gives  

\[
A(z)B(z)=z^{k}+z^{\ell}=z^{\ell}\bigl(z^{|k-\ell|}+1\bigr),
\]

and since monomials are units in \(\mathbb Z[z,z^{-1}]\) this is equivalent to \(A(z)\mid(z^{|k-\ell|}+1)\).  Thus a shifty \(\alpha\) corresponds precisely to an integer‑coefficient divisor (up to sign) of some binomial \(z^{m}+1\) with \(\deg A\le8\).

My current finding is that every shifty function corresponds to a polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}
\]

that **exactly divides a binomial** \(1+x^{q}\) (up to a monomial unit), i.e.  

\[
A(x)=x^{r}C(x),\qquad C(x)\mid(1+x^{q})\text{ in }\mathbb Z[x],\;0\le r\le 8-\deg C,
\]

with \(C(0)=\pm1\) and \(\deg C\le8\).  Consequently the problem reduces to enumerating all integer‑coefficient divisors \(C(x)\) of some \(1+x^{q}\) whose degree ≤ 8; each such \(C\) yields \(8-\deg C+1\) admissible shifts (and both signs), and no other \(\alpha\) can satisfy the shifty condition.  This gives a finite, explicit counting problem.

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a polynomial \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\) that can be written as  

\[
A(x)=x^{r}\,B(x),\qquad r\in\{0,\dots,8\},
\]

where the “core’’ factor \(B(x)\in\mathbb Z[x]\) has non‑zero constant term and **must divide a binomial \(1+x^{d}\) for some positive integer \(d\)** (i.e. \(B\mid 1+x^{d}\) in \(\mathbb Z[x]\)).  Equivalently, \(B\) is a product of cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{2^{e}m}\) with \(e\ge1\) and \(m\) odd, and \(\deg A\le8\).  This reduces the original functional condition to the purely algebraic divisibility problem above.

My current finding is that a shifty \(\alpha\) exists **iff** its generating polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\in\mathbb Z[x]
\]

satisfies  

\[
A(x)\mid\bigl(1+x^{q}\bigr)\qquad\text{for some }q\ge1,
\]

up to a monomial factor: \(A(x)=x^{r}C(x)\) where \(C(0)=\pm1\), \(\deg C\le8\) and \(C(x)\mid(1+x^{q})\).  Consequently the problem reduces to enumerating all integer‑coefficient divisors \(C\) of some binary cyclotomic polynomial \(1+x^{q}\) of degree \(\le8\); each such \(C\) yields \(8-\deg C+1\) admissible shifts (and both signs).  No other \(\alpha\) can satisfy the shifty condition.

My current finding is that a shifty α corresponds exactly to a **shifted divisor** of a binomial: if \(A(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)z^{i}=z^{r}C(z)\) with \(r\ge0\) and \(C(0)\neq0\), then the shifty condition is equivalent to the existence of an integer \(m>0\) such that  

\[
C(z)\mid (z^{m}+1)\qquad\text{in }\mathbb Z[z].
\]

Conversely, any divisor \(C(z)\) of some \(z^{m}+1\) (including \(\pm1\)) yields a shifty α by multiplying \(C(z)\) by any monomial \(z^{r}\) with \(0\le r\le 8-\deg C\) so that all exponents stay in \(\{0,\dots,8\}\). Thus shifty functions are precisely the polynomials obtained by taking a divisor of a binomial \(z^{m}+1\) and shifting it by a monomial factor that fits inside the interval \([0,8]\). This corrects the earlier claim “\(A(z)\mid(z^{m}+1)\) in \(\mathbb Z[z]\)” which fails for shifted (non‑constant‑term) polynomials.

My current finding is that a shifty \(\alpha\) exists **iff** its generating polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\in\mathbb Z[x]
\]

is a product of distinct cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{r}(x)\) whose indices \(r\) are even **and all have the same 2‑adic valuation** (i.e. \(r=2^{e}m\) with the same exponent \(e\ge1\) for every factor).  Moreover the total degree \(\sum_{r}\varphi(r)\) must be \(\le8\).  Consequently the admissible factors are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
e=1:&\;r\in\{2,6,10,14,18,30\},\;\varphi=1,2,4,6,6,8,\\
e=2:&\;r\in\{4,12,20\},\;\varphi=2,4,8,\\
e=3:&\;r\in\{8,24\},\;\varphi=4,8,\\
e=4:&\;r=16,\;\varphi=8.
\end{aligned}
\]

Any subset of a single line whose \(\varphi\)‑sum does not exceed 8 yields a valid \(A(x)\); the empty set gives \(A(x)=1\).  This reduction to “choose a subset of even‑indexed cyclotomic polynomials with equal 2‑adic exponent and total totient ≤ 8’’ is the key step for counting shifty functions.

My current finding is that a shifty α is exactly a polynomial \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\) of the form  

\[
A(x)=x^{r}\,B(x),\qquad 0\le r\le8,
\]

where \(B(0)\neq0\) and **\(B(x)\) divides \(1+x^{d}\) in \(\mathbb Z[x]\) for some integer \(d>0\)**.  Equivalently, \(B\) is a product of cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{2^{e}m}(x)\) with a fixed exponent‑of‑2 \(e\ge1\) and odd \(m\), and \(\deg B\le8-r\).  Thus every shifty function is obtained by taking a divisor of a binomial \(x^{d}+1\) (with degree ≤ 8) and optionally shifting it by a monomial \(x^{r}\).  This reduces the counting problem to enumerating all such divisor‑polynomials \(B\) (including the sign) and all admissible shifts \(r\).

My current finding is that the set of admissible \(\alpha\) is exactly the set of integer polynomials \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^8\alpha(i)x^i\) that, up to a monomial factor \(x^r\) (\(0\le r\le8-\deg C\)), equal a divisor \(C(x)\) of a binary cyclotomic polynomial \(1+x^q\) (i.e. \(C(x)\mid 1+x^q\) in \(\mathbb Z[x]\) with \(C(0)=\pm1\) and \(\deg C\le8\)); each such \(C\) yields \(8-\deg C+1\) shifts and both signs, and no other \(\alpha\) can satisfy the shifty condition. This reduces the counting problem to enumerating all divisors of \(1+x^q\) of degree ≤ 8.

My current finding is that a shifty α is exactly a **shifted divisor of a binomial**: if  

\[
A(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)z^{i}=z^{r}C(z),\qquad r\ge0,\;C(0)\neq0,
\]

then the shifty condition ⇔ there exists an integer \(m>0\) with  

\[

\]

Conversely, any divisor \(C(z)\) of some \(z^{m}+1\) (including \(\pm1\)) yields a shifty α by multiplying \(C(z)\) by any monomial \(z^{r}\) with \(0\le r\le 8-\deg C\); the sign ± gives a distinct α. This corrects the earlier claim “\(A(z)\mid(z^{m}+1)\) in \(\mathbb Z[z]\)’’ which fails for shifted (non‑constant‑term) polynomials.

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\in\mathbb Z[x]
\]

is a product of distinct cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{r}(x)\) whose indices \(r\) are even **and all have the same 2‑adic valuation** (i.e. \(r=2^{e}m\) with the same exponent \(e\ge1\) for every factor), and the total degree \(\sum_{r}\varphi(r)\le8\).  The admissible factors are

My current finding is that every shifty function corresponds uniquely to a pair \((r,B)\) where  

\[
0\le r\le8,\qquad B(x)\in\mathbb Z[x],\;B(0)=\pm1,\;\deg B\le8-r,
\]

and \(B\) divides a binomial \(1+x^{d}\) for some \(d>0\).  Equivalently, \(B\) is a product of distinct cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{2^{e}m}(x)\) (with a fixed exponent‑of‑2 \(e\ge1\) and odd \(m\)).  The polynomial of the shifty function is then \(A(x)=x^{r}B(x)\); this representation is unique because \(r\) is the smallest index with \(\alpha(r)\neq0\).  Consequently the total number of shifty functions equals  

\[
\sum_{B}\bigl(9-\deg B\bigr),
\]

where the sum runs over all such divisors \(B\) (including both signs).  This reduces the original functional problem to enumerating all products of cyclotomic factors of degree ≤ 8 with a common 2‑adic exponent.

My current finding is that the cyclotomic factors that can appear in any divisor \(C(x)\) of a binary polynomial \(1+x^{q}\) with \(\deg C\le8\) are **exactly**  

\[
\Phi_{2},\Phi_{4},\Phi_{6},\Phi_{8},\Phi_{10},\Phi_{12},
\Phi_{14},\Phi_{16},\Phi_{18},\Phi_{20},\Phi_{24},\Phi_{30},
\]

whose degrees are \(\phi(2)=1,\phi(4)=2,\phi(6)=2,\phi(8)=4,\phi(10)=4,\phi(12)=4,\phi(14)=6,\phi(16)=8,\phi(18)=6,\phi(20)=8,\phi(24)=8,\phi(30)=8\).  

For a fixed exponent of 2 in \(q\) (say \(q=2^{e}m\) with \(m\) odd) all factors have the same power‑of‑2 part \(2^{e+1}\); thus any admissible \(C\) is a product (up to sign) of a **subset of the above cyclotomics sharing the same \(2^{e+1}\) factor**, and its degree must be ≤ 8. This completely characterises the possible \(C\)’s, and hence all shifty \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds **bijectively** to a pair \((r,B)\) where  

\[
0\le r\le8,\qquad B(x)=\pm\!\!\prod_{i\in S}\Phi_{2^{e}m_i}(x)
\]

with a **fixed** exponent‑of‑2 \(e\ge1\), each \(m_i\) odd, the set \(S\) arbitrary, and  

\[
\deg B=2^{e}\!\sum_{i\in S}\varphi(m_i)\le 8-r .
\]

Equivalently, \(B\) is any divisor (up to sign) of a binomial \(1+x^{d}\) whose degree ≤ 8, and \(A(x)=x^{r}B(x)\) is the generating polynomial of α. Thus the number of shifty functions is  

\[
\displaystyle\sum_{B}\bigl(9-\deg B\bigr),
\]

the sum taken over all such \(B\) (including both signs). This reduces the original functional problem to enumerating products of cyclotomic factors with a common 2‑adic exponent and total degree ≤ 8.

This corrects earlier claims that required \(A(z)\mid(z^{m}+1)\) in \(\mathbb Z[z]\) without the shift.

C(z)=\prod_{d\in D}\Phi_{2^{\,t+1}d}(z),\qquad\deg C=2^{t}\!\sum_{d\in D}\phi(d)\le8,
\]

where Φ is the cyclotomic polynomial; any shift r with 0≤r≤8−deg C gives α(z)=±z^{r}C(z). with a **fixed** exponent‑of‑2 \(e\in\{0,1,2,3\}\), each \(m_i\) odd, and

C(z)=\prod_{d\in D}\Phi_{2^{\,t+1}d}(z),\qquad\deg C=2^{t}\!\sum_{d\in D}\varphi(d)\le8,
